description: The Internet has no single inventor. It is a long chain: a military network, a common language, then the Web for human beings.

hero.hook: First a network built to survive a war. Then the whole world plugged in.

blocks.text: The Internet was not born from a lone genius in a garage. It was built collectively, across several decades.
Three simple stages are worth remembering: a first network (ARPANET), a common language (TCP/IP), then an easy interface (the Web).
In the late **1960s**, in the middle of the Cold War, the American military funded a project: link computers so they could keep talking even if part of the network was destroyed.

blocks.caption: ARPANET first connected a handful of American universities

blocks.text: That network was called **ARPANET**. Messages were cut into small packets that traveled by different routes. If one route went down, another took over.

For different networks to understand each other, they needed shared rules. **Vint Cerf** and **Bob Kahn** worked out the **TCP/IP** protocol, a language that says how to split up data, address it, and put it back together.

blocks.caption: Cerf and Kahn: the architects of the language of the Internet

blocks.text: On January 1, **1983**, ARPANET switched officially to TCP/IP. Many people treat that date as the technical “birth” of the Internet.
The Internet is the network itself. The **World Wide Web**, invented by **Tim Berners-Lee** at CERN in the early **1990s**, is the easy layer on top: pages, links, browsers.
Without the Web, the Internet would have stayed a tool for experts. With it, anyone can click.

sections.title: The Web makes the network human

blocks.text: Today the Internet carries email, video, banking, hospitals, GPS. It has created new problems too: disinformation, surveillance, the digital divide.
The Internet grew out of ARPANET, became universal thanks to TCP/IP, and became usable thanks to the Web. It is not one invention, it is a shared architecture.
